name: Pan-Islamism
info: Pan-Islamism is an internationalist political movement that advocates the unity of Muslims under one Islamic state, often a caliphate; it took modern form in the late 19th century against European colonial rule and shaped later Islamist politics.

facts.thinkers: Jamal al-Din al-Afghani (1839–1897), who sought Muslim unity against colonial occupation; Muhammad Abduh (1849–1905), his student, who favoured reform through religion and education; Rashid Rida (1865–1935), who argued for a restored caliphate under Sharia; the classical scholars al-Mawardi, al-Ghazali and Fakhr al-Din al-Razi, who used the term ummah politically; Sayyid Qutb, Abul Ala Maududi and Ayatollah Khomeini among the later Islamists; Necmettin Erbakan, a Turkish prime minister who championed a Pan-Islamic Union
facts.texts: al-Mawardi’s Al-Ahkam al-Sultaniyyah; al-Ghazali’s Fadiah al-Batinyah wa Fadail al-Mustazhariyah; Rashid Rida’s al-Khilafa aw al-Imama al-‘Uzma (“The Caliphate or the Exalted Imamate”), formulated in the 1920s, and his journal Al-Manar; Lothrop Stoddard’s The New World of Islam (1921)
facts.ideas: the ummah, the Muslim community, as the focus of allegiance and mobilisation; Muslim unity under one Islamic state, often a caliphate; the Quran and the sunnah as guide; Tawhid; religion rather than ethnicity or race as the basis of unity; opposition to nationalism; resistance to colonial rule
facts.today: The Organisation of Islamic Conference, which grew out of the Rabat summit of 1969, is a permanent body of Muslim states; the Muslim Brotherhood, Jamaat-e-Islami and Hizb-ut-Tahrir are among the movements that carry the idea; the Developing 8 Countries, founded in 1996, still meet and carry out moderate collaboration projects

t: Pan-Islamism holds that Muslims should be united under one Islamic state, often a caliphate, and puts the ummah, not ethnicity or race, at the centre of allegiance, which sets it apart from ideologies such as Pan-Arabism.

Its modern leaders were Jamal al-Din al-Afghani, Muhammad Abduh and Rashid Rida, who worked against European penetration of Muslim lands; Afghani sought change from above, Abduh from below through education, and Rida a restored caliphate.

After the abolition of the caliphate in 1924 Rida’s ideas mobilised Muslims, and Arab nationalists such as Nasser repressed pan-Islamist movements; after the Six-Day War the Rabat summit of 1969 led to the Organisation of Islamic Conference.
dyk: Lothrop Stoddard counted the Pan-Islamic press in 1921: in 1900 there were not more than 200 propagandist journals in the whole Islamic world, by 1906 there were 500, and in 1914 well over 1000.
ev: Sultan Abdul Hamid II promotes pan-Islamism in the Ottoman Empire to prevent secession movements of its Muslim peoples
Rashid Rida sets out his vision of Islamic unity in Al-Manar
The Pan-Islamic press has grown to well over 1000 journals, by Lothrop Stoddard’s count

The first summit of Muslim heads of state meets at Rabat and becomes the Organisation of Islamic Conference
The Iranian Revolution ousts Shah Mohammad Reza Pahlavi
The Afghan mujahideen, with major support from the United States, force the Soviet Union from Afghanistan

sections.origins:
Pan-Islamism is an internationalist and anti-nationalist political movement that advocates the unity of Muslims under one Islamic state, often a caliphate or an international organisation with Islamic principles. It draws inspiration from early Islam, the era of Muhammad and the Rashidun Caliphate, and from the Islamic Golden Age. Classical scholars such as al-Mawardi, al-Ghazali and Fakhr al-Din al-Razi had already used the term ummah in a political sense. Many scholars assert its doctrines can be seen as early as Islamic Iberia, the Emirate of Sicily and the Ottoman, Safavid and Mughal Empires.

In the 18th century several movements for puritanical Islamic renewal arose. The revivalist movements of Shah Wali Allah of Delhi (1702–1763), Muhammad Ibn ‘Abd al-Wahhab (1703–1792) and Uthman dan Fodio (1755–1816) are widely regarded as precursors of modern pan-Islamist thought.They called for scripture-based piety but were not politically concerned with the international situation of the Muslim world and did not call for the revival of an international Islamic entity, and their impact stayed local to West Africa, Arabia and South Asia.

Reformers at the turn of the 19th century oscillated between admiration for Western progress and rejection of it; Rifa‘a al-Tahtawi (d. 1872) exemplified the former, ‘Abd al-Rahman al-Jabarti (d. 1825) the latter. In the Ottoman Empire, after Ottomanism, which aimed at the unity of all Ottoman citizens, Sultan Abdul Hamid II promoted pan-Islamism in the last quarter of the 19th century to prevent secession movements among the empire’s Muslim peoples.
sections.ideas:
Pan-Islamism differs from nationalist ideologies such as Pan-Arabism by focusing on religion and not on ethnicity or race. It sees the ummah as the focus of allegiance and mobilisation, together with the belief in Tawhid, under the guidance of the Quran and the sunnah. The Arabic term ummah occurs in the Quran and Islamic tradition and has historically denoted the Muslims as a whole, regardless of race or ethnicity.

Jamal al-Din al-Afghani feared that nationalism would divide the Muslim world and held that Muslim unity mattered more than ethnic identity. Although sometimes called liberal, he did not advocate constitutional government; his biographer found nothing in his Paris-based newspaper that favoured political democracy or parliamentarianism, and he envisaged the overthrow of rulers who were lax or subservient to foreigners and their replacement by strong, patriotic men.

Rashid Rida believed that the unification of the Islamic community would be possible only through the restoration of a caliphate that implements the Sharia. In 1902 he wrote in Al-Manar that Islamic unity meant that the scholars and notables should compile a book of ordinances based on the fundamentals of the Divine Law, which a Supreme Imam would order the rulers of Muslims to apply. In the 1920s he set out a doctrine of the Islamic state in al-Khilafa aw al-Imama al-‘Uzma, calling on Muslims to build a political system based on faith rather than nationalism.
sections.spread:
Jamal al-Din al-Afghani, Muhammad Abduh and Rashid Rida were the major leaders of the modern movement, active in anti-colonial efforts against European penetration of Muslim lands, and they held Islamic unity to be the strongest force for mobilising Muslims against imperial domination. Rida’s Al-Manar promoted anti-British revolt and Islamic revivalism based on the tenets of Salafiyya. Lothrop Stoddard, in 1921, took the growth of the Pan-Islamic press as a measure of the movement’s rising importance, counting not more than 200 propagandist journals in 1900, 500 by 1906 and well over 1000 in 1914.

After the abolition of the caliphate in 1924, pan-Islamism mobilised Muslim masses of both traditionalist and reform movements, inspired by Rida. During the 1920s Rida and his Salafi disciples established the Young Men’s Muslim Association, an Islamist youth organisation. Pan-Islamic networks led by Rida and his associates played a central role in the later development of Islamist movements.

In the 1950s Pakistan’s government championed Muslim cooperation. After the Six-Day War, Islamism and pan-Islamism gained popularity relative to nationalism and Pan-Arabism, and in 1969 the first summit of Muslim heads of state met at Rabat. After 1979 the branches of the Muslim Brotherhood, Jamaat-e-Islami in Pakistan and, since the collapse of the Soviet Union, Hizb-ut-Tahrir in Central Asia became prominent pan-Islamist forces.
sections.power:
Pan-Islamism was used as state policy before it became a movement against states. Abdul Hamid II promoted it in the Ottoman Empire in the last quarter of the 19th century to hold the empire’s Muslim peoples together. Ibn Saud’s conquest of the Arabian Peninsula bolstered pan-Islamism across the Islamic world. At the height of the Cold War, in the 1960s and 1970s, Saudi Arabia and allied countries in the Muslim world led the pan-Islamist struggle against the spread of communist ideology and the rising Soviet influence in the world.

During the second half of the 20th century pan-Islamists competed against left-wing nationalist ideologies in the Arab world, such as Nasserism and Ba’athism. After the Second World War secular pan-Arab parties, Baath and Nasserist, had offshoots in almost every Arab country and took power in Egypt, Libya, Iraq and Syria. Islamists suffered severe repression: Sayyid Qutb was imprisoned, tortured and later executed. Egyptian president Nasser, who considered the idea of Muslim unity a threat to Arab nationalism, took control of the mosques and appointed his own religious officials, and the religious establishment he created denounced the Muslim Brotherhood as inauthentic representatives of Islam.

Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan founded the Developing 8 Countries in 1996, with Turkey, Egypt, Iran, Pakistan, Indonesia, Malaysia, Nigeria and Bangladesh, but his government was taken down by the so-called Post-Modern Coup of 28 February 1997.
sections.critiques:
Within the movement the founders disagreed. Abduh criticised Afghani and the pan-Islamist intellectuals for their political activities and judged education a more effective instrument of reform, while Afghani had bitter arguments with Abduh. The doctrines also divided Muslims on who should lead: Rida called for a caliphate led by Arabs, and after 1979 Sunni Islamists such as Maududi and the Muslim Brotherhood embraced a new caliphate as at least a long-term project, whereas Khomeini also embraced a united Islamic supra-state but saw it led by a Shia religious scholar of fiqh, a faqih.

Nationalists and secularists opposed the idea. Afghani feared that nationalism would divide the Muslim world, and Islamists in turn denounced nationalism as un-Islamic. In the period of decolonisation after the Second World War Arab nationalism overshadowed Islamism, and Nasser saw Muslim unity as a threat to Arab nationalism. After the First World War Rida and his disciples became the biggest adversaries of secularists and nationalists and vehemently attacked all forms of democratic ideas.

Governments were wary of one another’s pan-Islamic claims. Pakistan’s efforts in the 1950s were complicated by its part in the Baghdad Pact and its pro-Western diplomacy, and many Muslim countries suspected that Pakistan aspired to leadership of the Muslim world in order to help Western powers in their relations with other Muslim states. Later relations were much better.
sections.legacy:
The early pan-Islamist movement in the post-colonial world was strongly associated with Islamism. Rida’s socio-political views marked the convergence of the doctrines of the reformist, Salafist and pan-Islamist movements, and his networks played a central role in the later development of Islamist movements. After the defeat of the Arab armies in the Six-Day War, Nasser dropped his opposition to a pan-Islamic platform, and the Rabat summit of 1969 was eventually transformed into a permanent body, the Organisation of Islamic Conference.

The events of 1979 and 1989 galvanised Islamists the world over and heightened their popularity with the Muslim public. Branches of the Muslim Brotherhood challenged secular nationalist or monarchical Muslim governments throughout the Middle East, in particular in Egypt. In Pakistan Jamaat-e-Islami enjoyed popular support, especially since the formation of the MMA, and in Algeria the FIS was expected to win the elections cancelled in 1992. Since the collapse of the Soviet Union Hizb-ut-Tahrir has emerged as a pan-Islamist force in Central Asia.

Erbakan, a recent advocate, championed the Pan-Islamic Union, an Islamic Union (İslam Birliği), and his vision was a gradual unity of Muslim nations through economic and technological cooperation, similar to the European Union, with a single monetary unit and joint aerospace and defence projects. The Developing 8 Countries still meet at presidential and cabinet levels and moderate collaboration projects continue, though its momentum was lost after the coup of 1997.

summary: Pan-Islamism advocates the unity of Muslims under one Islamic state, often a caliphate, with the ummah rather than ethnicity as the focus of allegiance. It took modern form in the late 19th century with Afghani, Abduh and Rida, it later competed with Arab nationalism and led to the Organisation of Islamic Conference.
references: Jacob M. Landau, The Politics of Pan-Islam: Ideology and Organization (Clarendon Press, Oxford, 1990)
notes: Start 1875, circa true: the article dates the Ottoman promotion only to 'the last quarter of the 19th century' and Afghani's life to 1839–1897; no exact year is given for the modern movement's beginning.

The article does not describe a record in power beyond: Abdul Hamid II's policy, Saudi-led anti-communist effort, Nasser's repression of Islamists, Erbakan's D8 and the 1997 coup; the power section is built from those only.
'Dinarı' coinage and 'single monetary unit': kept as in the article. The article writes 'Pan-Islamic Union (İslam Birliği)'.

Event 1914: Stoddard's count is 'in 1914 well over 1000'; event 1902 date is the article's Al-Manar quotation. Event 1924: the abolition of the caliphate is dated only by the article's heading 'Abolition of Caliphate in 1924'.
The 'Late 19th century' event label is not a year; the article gives only 'last quarter of the 19th century'.

Legacy: 'in the last five years' (Hizb-ut-Tahrir support in the Arab world) is the article's own undated phrasing; kept in the text without a year, the editor may want to cut it. The article also says the Kharijite extremism goes back to the 7th century; left out as it is not tied to pan-Islamism.

Facts 'today': the article calls the body Organisation of Islamic Conference; left out later renamings as the article does not give them. 'Islamic Military Alliance' and the Murabitun World Movement appear only in the see-also list and are left out.

Article is thin on critiques; those given are the positions and suspicions the article reports. The article's garbled sentence on Pakistan 'to in foreword help western powers' was read as 'to help Western powers'; the editor should read it.
